messages.subject: [Mediation-information] A Question on Causal Mediation Analysis
messages.subject_clean: [Mediation-information] A Question on Causal Mediation Analysis
messages.body_plain:
Min-Young-

Thanks for your interest in using our package.

We have not yet implemented duration models into our package. In principle
it should be able to handle these but we have not yet done this. If you know
some R you can modify our code. Otherwise this will have to wait until a
future release.

One quick note, in our framework you need only two models (using your
notation, Y=M+X and M=X).

best,
Dustin

Dustin Tingley
Government Department
Harvard University
http://scholar.harvard.edu/dtingley



On Mon, Oct 3, 2011 at 1:48 PM, Min-Young Kim <mkim.uiuc at gmail.com> wrote:

> Dear Professor Dustin Tingley,****
>
> ** **
>
> I am writing this email to ask you a question on the ?Causal Mediation
> Analysis Using R?.****
>
> ** **
>
> I am a PhD candidate at the business school of the University of Illinois
> at Urbana-Champaign. ****
>
> ** **
>
> I am currently working on a project in which I employ a mediation analysis.
> But I am facing some difficulties due to the nature of my mediating
> variable.****
>
> ** **
>
> The following is a brief outline of the mediation model.****
>
> ** **
>
> **1.      **X: a count variable (the number of countries)****
>
> **2.      **M: time (time taken to first forward citation in patent
> citation network)****
>
> **3.      **Y: a count variable (the number of citations a patent
> receives)****
>
> ** **
>
> Due to the various data types, I am estimating with:****
>
> **1.      **A negative binomial model for X->Y****
>
> **2.      **An accelerated-failure time (AFT) model (one of the survival
> models) for X->M****
>
> **3.      **A negative binomial model for M->Y****
>
> ** **
>
> As many of the current statistical models for mediating analyses are
> developed for continues mediating and/or dependent variables, I am
> experiencing difficult time in testing my hypotheses.****
>
> ** **
>
> In the meantime, I have found that ?A Question on Causal Mediation Analysis
> Using R? could help me dealing with these issues.****
>
> ** **
>
> But when reading through the instruction manual, especially Table 1 in page
> 9 (of the version September 19, 2011), I found that that accelerated-failure
> time model is not included in the mediator model type.****
>
> ** **
>
> So, my question is:****
>
> **1.      **Whether it is possible to test my mediation hypotheses with
> your ?mediate? program for R?****
>
> **2.      **if not, do you have any plan to include the AFT model in the
> ?mediate? program?****
>
> ** **
>
> Any comments would be really appreciated.****
>
> ** **
>
> Thank you so much.****
>
> ** **
>
> Sincerely yours,****
>
> ** **
>
> Min-Young Kim****
>
> ** **
>

messages.subject: [Mediation-information] interpretation for mediation effect
messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

I have one more question about the interpretation of the Proportion of Total
Effect via Mediation (Average). For example in the following result,
*Proportion of Total Effect via Mediation (Average):*  *-0.1391* 95 % CI
-1.7258  0.8114
Does it mean the 13.91% of total effect is mediated by the mediator? Can
I interpret the proportion here as a percentage?

Thanks a lot.

Sincerely,
Weichao

On Thu, Sep 15, 2011 at 10:55 AM, Weichao Bao <weichaobao at gmail.com> wrote:

> Dear All,
>
>
> I am using the mediation package on my research. The outcome is dichotomous
> and the treatment is continuous. It was run with GAM model.  But I am
> confused with the following results. It shows all the Mediation
> Effect_0, Mediation Effect_1,and Mediation Effect (Average) have significant
> mediation effect based on 95% CI. However, the Proportion of Total Effect
> via Mediation_0, Proportion of Total Effect via Mediation_1, and Proportion
> of Total Effect via Mediation (Average) indicate there is no mediation at
> all based on the 95% confidence interval.  The result is:
>
>
> Mediation Effect_0:  -0.004309 95 % CI  -0.0086640 -0.0007235
>
> Mediation Effect_1:  -0.006557 95 % CI  -0.014173 -0.001015
>
> Direct Effect_0:  0.04452 95 % CI  0.001001 0.112969
>
> Direct Effect_1:  0.04228 95 % CI  0.0009312 0.1061973
>
> Total Effect:  0.03797 95 % CI  -0.004335  0.101359
>
> Proportion of Total Effect via Mediation_0:  -0.1069 95 % CI  -1.592
> 0.817
>
> Proportion of Total Effect via Mediation_1:  -0.1701 95 % CI  -1.8595  0.8059
>
>
> Mediation Effect (Average):  -0.005433 95 % CI  -0.011059 -0.000928
>
> Direct Effect (Average):  0.0434 95 % CI  0.0009659 0.1098405
>
> Proportion of Total Effect via Mediation (Average):  -0.1391 95 % CI
> -1.7258  0.8114
>
>
> Can somebody help me to explain this?
>
>
> Thanks a lot.
>
> Sincerely,
>
>
> Weichao
>
>
>

messages.subject: [Mediation-information] interpretation for mediation effect
messages.body_plain:
This quantity is defined as:

(Total Effect - ACME) / Total Effect

And so in your case, it looks like the direct effect has the opposite sign.

Kosuke

Department of Politics
Princeton University
http://imai.princeton.edu

messages.subject: [Mediation-information] Question about mediation package in two level design
messages.subject_clean: [Mediation-information] Question about mediation package in two level design
messages.body_plain:
Hi Sun Yoon,

 Unfortunately, the current version of our package does not incorporate multi-level models (if that's what you are using).  However, if you know some programming, then implementing our general algorithm as described in our Psychological Methods paper should be in principle straightforward: http://imai.princeton.edu/research/BaronKenny.html   I'm ccing Michael Donnelly who used mixed effects models for mediation in case he can share some of his codes. 

Good luck,
Kosuke

Department of Politics
Princeton University
http://imai.princeton.edu

> Dear professor Kosuke Imai,
> 
> Hi, my name is Sun, a doctoral student in the Educational Leadership and Policy Analysis department at University of Wisconsin-Madison. I 
> greatly appreciate your effort and contribution on your works. While I'm investigating the mediation analysis on my study, gladly I found "mediation" R package and your papers which I appreciate. But I have some questions about "mediation" package in multi level design. 
> 
> My current study is a randomized cluster experimental design and I am investigating the mediating effect between treatment and outcome. Mediation variable is a count variable in level 2, an independent variable is binary variable inlevel 2, and outcome variable is continuous in level 1. I found that you demonstrated the count mediation variable in the design, but I'm not sure whether I could still use that model in cluster design too. I'd sincerely appreciate it if you could suggest any ideas or reference. I look forward to hearing from you soon. Thank you.
> 
> Best wishes,
> 
> Sun Yoon

> --

messages.subject: [Mediation-information] Causal mediation analysis?
messages.body_plain:
Ho-Chuan,

  It is only applicable in the sense that conditional on pre-treatment covariates the treatment assignment must be ignorable.  If that condition is not met, then causal mediation analysis will be biased.   So, the key is to collect confounding variables so that the treatment can be assumed to be as-if random given those variables.

Kosuke

Department of Politics
Princeton University
http://imai.princeton.edu


On Oct 23, 2011, at 11:05 PM, River wrote:

> Dear Professor Imai,
>  
> I find that many of your papers related to causal mediation analysis are interesting and helpful. However, I wonder if the approach is applicable to the case where the assignment to treatment and control is nonrandom. For example, suppose that I am interested in measuring the macro-economic (treatment) effects (and the corresponding causal mechanisms) of inflation targeting (IT). However, it is well known that the choice of implementing the IT framework is self-selected by the central bankers and unlikely to be random.
